title: Reading Yourself Under Stress
hook: Under pressure your body announces your state before your thoughts do, and most men have spent years learning not to hear it.
why:
Every protocol in this book begins with reading yourself, and in calm moments that is easy: a breath, a check of the shoulders, a question about what you want to be true. The difficulty is that the moments when reading yourself matters most are the moments of stress, and stress is exactly when you are least able to do it. Your heart rate rises, your breath climbs, your jaw sets, and your thoughts, which arrive a little later, are already busy with the other person.

This chapter is about reading yourself in those moments, as a reader of other people. It is not the chapter on interoception or on early warning signs for your mental health; Part II covers those. Its question is narrower: how your own stress changes what you see in others, and what you can do about it in the minute it is happening. It teaches you to treat your sense of your own body as a reading that needs calibrating, to map your personal stress signature, to name and reappraise what you feel, to use your breath, and to correct the readings you make while the signature is running.

teach.p:
The stress response is fast. Within seconds of a threat, your heart speeds up, your breathing becomes quicker and higher in the chest, muscles in your jaw, neck and shoulders tighten, and your hands look for something to hold. The conscious appraisal, the thought that says *this is an attack* or *I am being humiliated*, tends to follow. By the time you know you are stressed, your body has usually been saying so for a while.

That gap is an opportunity, because the early bodily signs can warn you before your thoughts have committed you to a reading of the other person. It is also a problem, because many men have spent years learning not to notice those signs.

The psychologist Ronald Levant has argued that many boys are taught, by example and by shaming, to stop noticing and naming feelings that seem soft or weak, a pattern he called normative male alexithymia. Studies have found that men, on average, score somewhat higher than women on measures of difficulty identifying and describing feelings. The difference is modest, and it varies enormously between individuals, but the mechanism is familiar. A boy told to stop crying learns to stop noticing what came before the crying, and the habit lasts.

For a reader of people, the cost is direct. The signs you have learned not to hear are the ones that would tell you your reading of someone else is about to be bent by your own state. If you only notice your anger when you hear your raised voice, you have already read the other person through it.

The work of this chapter is to hear the body earlier. Not to obey it, and not to silence it: to hear it in time.
teach.disconfirm: If you find, when you compare your journal with video or with an honest friend's account, that you reliably notice your own stress before anyone else could see it, your early warning is already working. Check it on your three most stressful moments of the past month, not your average ones.

teach.h: Being sure about your body is not reading it.
teach.p:
You might assume that you at least know your own body. The research suggests caution. In 2015 Sarah Garfinkel, Anil Seth and their colleagues distinguished three things that are easily run together. Interoceptive accuracy is how well you actually detect signals from inside your body, measured for example by how well you can track your own heartbeat. Interoceptive sensibility is how good you believe you are at it. Interoceptive awareness is whether your confidence matches your accuracy. They found that the three can come apart: people who believe they are very attuned to their bodies are not necessarily accurate, and some accurate people have little confidence in it.

The measurement itself is debated. The classic heartbeat-counting task, in which people silently count their heartbeats over a period and the count is compared with the true number, has been criticised because many people estimate rather than feel. That uncertainty is itself the lesson. Your felt sense of your own state is a reading, made with imperfect instruments, and it needs the same calibration as your readings of other people.

So treat your report of your own state as a hypothesis. *I'm calm* is a claim. Check it against something observable: a recording of yourself from the video review chapter, an honest mirror's account from the feedback chapter, or a simple physical measure such as your pulse or the number of breaths you take in a minute.

Over a few weeks you will find out where your sense of yourself is reliable and where it is not. Most people find that they notice some signs early and are almost blind to others.
teach.disconfirm: If, over two weeks, your ratings of your own arousal closely track your measured pulse and breathing, and agree with what others see, your sense of your own state is well calibrated. Keep checking it in high-stakes moments, where it is most likely to drift.
teach.pullQuote: Your felt sense of your own state is a reading, and it needs calibrating like any other.

teach.p:
Stress shows itself differently in different people, and fairly consistently within each person. One man's jaw sets and his blinking stops. Another's voice climbs and quickens. A third goes very still and quiet, which others may read as calm. The pattern, and especially its order, is your stress signature, and knowing it lets you catch the response at its first sign rather than its last.

Build it from evidence rather than from memory. Take three journal entries from moments when you were clearly stressed and, for each, write down every bodily change you can recall, in the order it came. Then check against any outside evidence you have. Video review is the best: watch a recording of yourself in a tense moment and note what happens to your face, breath, hands and voice, second by second. An honest mirror is the next best: ask someone who knows you well what they see in you just before you lose your temper or go quiet.

Look for the earliest reliable sign. It is often small and away from the face, because the face is what you have learned to manage: a tightening in the stomach, a foot that starts to move, the urge to pick something up, a slight lean forward. That earliest sign is the trigger for the if-then plans of the protocol chapter.

Notice too that the signature may differ by kind of stress. Anger, fear and shame often feel similar in the first seconds and run differently afterwards. Many men discover that what they had always called anger begins, in the body, as shame.

Write the signature as a short sequence, earliest first, and keep it at the front of your journal.
teach.disconfirm: If, after mapping your signature, you find that it does not appear in the same order or with the same signs in your next three stressful moments, either it varies with the kind of stress or the map was built from memory rather than evidence. Map each kind separately, using video where you can.

teach.p:
Putting a feeling into words changes it. In 2007 Matthew Lieberman and colleagues scanned people's brains while they looked at pictures of emotional faces. When participants chose a word to label the emotion in a face, activity in the amygdala, a region involved in threat responses, was lower than when they chose a name or simply looked. Later work extended the finding beyond the scanner. In a 2012 study by Katharina Kircanski, Lieberman and Michelle Craske, people afraid of spiders who described their feelings out loud while approaching a spider showed less physiological arousal when they faced it again a week later than those who used other strategies.

Precision seems to matter. Research by Todd Kashdan, Lisa Feldman Barrett and Patrick McKnight, reviewed in 2015, found that people who draw finer distinctions between their negative feelings, telling apart irritation, disappointment, embarrassment and shame rather than lumping them together as feeling bad, tend to cope better under stress. They are, for example, less likely to drink heavily or lash out when hurt.

For a reader in the middle of a hard conversation, this suggests a small, private act. When your signature fires, name the feeling to yourself, in one precise word: *embarrassed*, *cornered*, *ashamed*, *afraid*. Do not say it aloud unless that would help the conversation. The aim is not to explain the feeling or to get rid of it. It is to give it a name, so that it becomes something you have rather than something that has you.

A precise name also tells you something about your reading of the other person. If the feeling is shame, the threat you are reading in them may be the judgment you fear rather than anything they have shown.
teach.disconfirm: If silently naming the feeling makes no difference to how intense it is or how you respond, compared with not naming it, across a dozen moments, the technique is not working for you in that form. Try naming it in writing straight afterwards, or aloud to someone you trust.

teach.h: Reappraise the arousal, don't fight it.
teach.p:
The usual advice under stress is to calm down. The evidence suggests that telling yourself to relax is often less useful than changing what you take the arousal to mean.

In 2012 Jeremy Jamieson, Matthew Nock and Wendy Berry Mendes gave people a stressful public-speaking task. Before it, some were told that the signs of arousal they would feel, such as a racing heart and faster breathing, were the body's way of preparing to perform well, and that the arousal could help them. Compared with people given no such message, those who reappraised their arousal showed a healthier pattern of cardiovascular response, with the heart pumping more efficiently and the blood vessels less constricted, and they were less drawn to threatening information. In 2014 Alison Wood Brooks found that people who said *I am excited* before singing, speaking or doing mental arithmetic in front of others performed better than those who said *I am calm* or *I am anxious*.

The point is not that stress is good. It is that the same bodily state can be read as threat or as readiness, and the reading shapes what the body does next. That is the logic of this whole book turned inward. A racing heart, like crossed arms, has more than one meaning, and you get to test the more useful one.

In practice, when your signature fires in a hard conversation, follow the silent label with a reappraisal: *This is my body getting ready. It can help me pay attention.* Then use the arousal on the task in front of you, which is to listen.

Do not use reappraisal to talk yourself out of real danger. If the arousal is telling you to leave, leave.
teach.disconfirm: If reframing your arousal as readiness leaves your heart rate, your voice and your readings of other people exactly as they were, the reframe is not doing anything for you in those situations. Compare a few moments with and without it, using your journal and, if you can, a pulse reading.

teach.h: Breath is the lever you can reach.
teach.p:
Of all the signs in your stress signature, breath is unusual. It runs automatically, and you can also take control of it at will. That makes it the most direct way you have of acting on your own state in the middle of a conversation, without anyone noticing.

The evidence supports a modest claim. A 2018 review by Andrea Zaccaro and colleagues found that slow breathing, at fewer than ten breaths a minute and often around six, was associated with signs of greater parasympathetic activity, the branch of the nervous system involved in rest, and with people reporting more relaxation and less anxiety and anger. In 2023 Melis Yilmaz Balban, David Spiegel, Andrew Huberman and colleagues compared several five-minute daily breathing practices with mindfulness meditation over a month. A practice they called the cyclic sigh, two inhalations through the nose followed by a long, slow exhalation through the mouth, produced the largest improvement in mood and the largest fall in breathing rate at rest. The study was small, and the claims for any one technique should be held lightly.

What the studies have in common is the long exhalation. For use in the moment, that is enough: one slow breath out, longer than the breath in, before you answer a hard question. In a pause, two or three such breaths. Nobody across the table will see it, and it gives both your body and your reading a few seconds to settle.

Practise it when nothing is at stake, a few minutes a day, so that it is available when something is.

Breathing will not make a hard conversation easy. It will make you a little more present for it.
teach.disconfirm: If several weeks of slow breathing practice leave your measured breathing rate, your pulse in tense moments and your sense of steadiness unchanged, breath is not the lever that works best for you. Your stress signature may suggest another, such as relaxing your hands or feet.

teach.h: Read others through a stressed lens, then correct.
teach.p:
Stress changes what you see in other people, not only how you feel. Research on anxiety has found, again and again, a bias in interpretation: anxious people are more likely to read ambiguous faces and situations as threatening. The statement at the front of this book described Joseph Forgas's finding that feelings seep into judgments of other people most strongly when the information is ambiguous. Stress is the strongest form of that seepage, and most readings of people are ambiguous.

So the readings you make while your signature is running deserve their own handling. Tag them in your journal and your ledger with your state at the time, as the calibration chapter suggested, and look at their calibration separately. Most readers find that their readings of hostility, contempt or rejection made under stress are markedly less accurate than the same readings made calm.

Then make a rule from what you find. A common one is this: a reading made while the signature is active is held at one band less confidence than it feels, is not acted on in the moment if action can wait, and is rechecked once you have settled. In practice that means a sentence ready for the moment you need it: *Let me think about that properly and come back to you this afternoon.*

Afterwards, when you are calm, look again at what you saw. Ask what the other person did, as behaviour, and what else it could have meant. Very often the reading softens. Sometimes it holds, and then you can act on it with a clearer head.

Never let your stress make a decision about another person that your calm self has not reviewed.
teach.disconfirm: If your ledger shows that readings you made under stress are as well calibrated as readings made calm, stress does not bend your readings much in that domain. Check separately for readings of hostility and rejection, where the bias usually shows most.

caseStudy:
Nathan, thirty-six, is a senior engineer who leads design reviews at a software company. He is good at the work and dreaded in the reviews. When his own designs are criticised, he reads colleagues as hostile and snaps. Two people have asked to move teams.

After the video review chapter he records, with everyone's agreement, two of his own reviews. Watching them is unpleasant. He maps his signature from the recordings and from his partner, who has seen it at home for years. First his jaw sets and he stops blinking. Then his breathing moves high into his chest. Then he starts typing on his laptop, though he is not writing anything. Then his speech speeds up and he begins to interrupt. By the time he hears himself interrupting, it is too late.

He chooses the jaw as his trigger. When it sets, he names the feeling silently. To his surprise, the word that fits is almost always *ashamed*, not *angry*. He follows it with one long breath out and a reappraisal: *this is my body getting ready; use it to listen*. And he has a sentence ready for when he cannot answer calmly: *Let me look at that properly and come back to you this afternoon.*

In March, in a review of a design he is proud of, Rosa, the most senior architect, frowns hard at his diagram and says nothing for a long time. He feels his jaw set. The old reading arrives at once: contempt. He names it, ashamed, breathes out, and asks, *What are you seeing?*

Rosa says there is a race condition in the cache, and she has been tracing it. Then she says the rest of the design is the best she has reviewed this year.

That night Nathan checks his ledger. Of ten readings of a colleague as hostile that he made with his signature running, eight were wrong.
observe: The next time a conversation becomes difficult, notice the very first change in your body, before you have formed any thought about the other person.
Notice one moment this week when you said or thought I'm fine while some part of your body was telling you something else.
After a tense exchange, notice how your reading of the other person changes once your breathing has settled.

drills.name: Signature Map
steps: Choose three journal entries from moments when you were clearly stressed.
For each, list every bodily change you can recall, in the order it came.
Check the lists against any video of yourself or an honest friend's account, and correct them.
Mark the earliest sign that appears in at least two of the three.
Write your signature as a short sequence, earliest first, at the front of your journal.

drills.name: Body Report Check
steps: Three times a day, rate your arousal from one to ten and note the sign you are basing it on.
Immediately check your pulse for thirty seconds, or count your breaths for one minute.
Write both numbers down side by side.
Repeat for a week, including at least one tense moment.
At the end of the week, note where your ratings matched the measures and where they did not.

drills.name: Silent Label
steps: Write a list of at least ten precise words for difficult feelings, such as irritated, embarrassed, cornered, ashamed, disappointed and afraid.
In mildly stressful moments this week, such as traffic, queues or a difficult email, name the feeling silently with one word from the list.
Notice whether its intensity changes in the next half minute.
Log each label and the situation.
At the end of the week, write which labels recur and whether any surprised you.

drills.name: Long Exhale
steps: Sit comfortably and breathe in through your nose for a slow count of four.
Breathe out through your mouth for a slow count of eight.
Continue for five minutes, letting the count lengthen if it is comfortable.
Repeat once a day for a fortnight, at a time when nothing is at stake.
Then use a single long exhalation before answering in your next three tense conversations, and note what happened.

drills.name: State-Tagged Ledger
steps: Tag each scored prediction in your ledger as made with your signature running or made calm.
Draw the calibration curve for each tag separately.
Look especially at readings of hostility, contempt or rejection.
Write a rule based on any gap you find, such as holding stressed readings at one band less confidence.
Write your sentence for postponing a response, and practise saying it aloud.

quiz.q: You feel confident that you always know when you are stressed. What does the research on interoception suggest about that confidence?
options: That confidence about your body tracks how accurately you can sense it
That confidence and accuracy in sensing your body can come quite apart
That men tend to sense their own bodies more accurately than women do
That only trained athletes can sense their own bodily states with real accuracy
quiz.explain: Garfinkel and colleagues separated accuracy, confidence and the match between them, and found they can diverge. Treat your sense of your own state as a reading to check against video, an honest mirror or a simple measure.

quiz.q: What did Lieberman and colleagues find when people put feelings into words while looking at emotional faces?
options: Activity in the amygdala was lower than when they did not label
Labelling the feeling made it stronger and longer-lasting than before
Labelling the feeling had no measurable effect on the brain at all
Labelling only helped people who had already been through therapy
quiz.explain: Choosing a word for the emotion reduced activity in a region involved in threat responses. Later studies found related benefits outside the scanner, and precise labels seem to help more than vague ones.

quiz.q: In Jamieson, Nock and Mendes's study, what helped people facing a stressful speaking task?
options: Being told to suppress every sign of nervousness they felt
Being told to relax completely before the task began
Being given extra time to prepare for the task alone and in private
Being told their arousal was the body preparing them to perform
quiz.explain: Reappraising arousal as useful produced a healthier cardiovascular response and less pull towards threat. The bodily state was the same; what it was taken to mean changed what the body did next.

quiz.q: In a review of your work, a senior colleague frowns hard at your design and says nothing. You feel your jaw set and your breath rise. What fits?
options: Respond straight away and firmly, before the moment passes
Defend the design hard, since a frown like that shows open contempt for it
Name the feeling silently, breathe out, and ask what she is seeing
Say nothing and leave the review as soon as you reasonably can
quiz.explain: Your signature has fired, which is when your reading of her is most likely to lean towards threat. Naming the feeling and a long exhale give you a few seconds, and an open question tests the reading instead of acting on it.

quiz.q: Which is the most honest summary of the evidence on slow breathing with long exhalations?
options: It cures anxiety completely after a few weeks of daily practice
It works only for people who have also been taught to meditate
It has been shown to have no measurable effect on the body at all
Small studies suggest it tends to lower arousal and improve mood
quiz.explain: Reviews and small trials point the same way, towards lower arousal and better mood, but the studies are modest in size. That is enough to make a long breath out worth using, and not enough to promise more.

quiz.q: You realise you have formed a strong reading of a colleague as hostile while your stress signature was at its peak. What fits?
options: Hold it at one band less confidence, and recheck it once you have settled
Act on it now, since stress sharpens perception of other people's threat
Discard it entirely, since readings made under stress are always wrong
Tell the colleague at once what you read in them, so it is in the open
quiz.explain: Stress biases readings towards threat, especially when the evidence is ambiguous, but it does not make them always wrong. Holding the reading loosely, postponing action and rechecking it calm is the correction.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment in the past month when stress changed how you read someone: a partner, a colleague, a stranger. What was the first sign in your body, and when did you notice it, if you did? What did you conclude about the other person at the time, and how did that reading look once you had calmed down? Which part of your stress signature would you most like to catch earlier next time, and what would you do in the seconds after catching it?
reflection.guidance: Many men find the first question the hardest, because they noticed the stress only when they heard their own voice. That is useful information: it tells you how late your current warning comes. Name the feeling as precisely as you can, and notice whether the word you reach for first is the right one. Anger is often the second feeling, not the first.

failureMode: One failure is to turn this chapter into constant self-monitoring, checking your pulse and scanning your body all day, which raises the very arousal it is meant to manage. Another is to use labels and breathing as a way of pushing feelings down rather than hearing them, so that *I'm fine* simply becomes a quieter, better-managed *I'm fine*. A third is to reappraise away real danger, telling yourself the racing heart is excitement when it is warning you to leave. A fourth is to read this as a matter of willpower and to decide that a real man should not need it. If your stress signs are frequent, persistent, or disturbing your sleep, work or relationships, the chapters of Part II and a doctor are the right next step, not more technique.
